To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the electronic and molecular structure, as well as the PH orientation, of the 233 and 265 residue constructs of human hHO are essentially identical, that the steric tilt for the Fe-CN unit in the 233-residue construct is approximately 2 degrees less than for the 265-residue construct, and that the steric transition of PH into a hydrophobic pocket in the cyanide-inhibibted complex is approximately 1 A greater for rat HO than human hHO.

the electronic and molecular structure in the PH substrate complex of hHO is essentially the same for both the 233- or 265-residue constructs, the equilibrium distribution of PH orientational isomers changes from 1:1 for the water-ligated resting-state complex to a 4.5:1 equilibrium for the cyanide-inhibibited complex, with the major isomer in the cyanide-inhibition complex corresponding to the only isomer found in crystals, and the steric tilt angle

the active site electronic structure of heme oxygenase is not perturbed by the presence of the substrate, and the molecular structure is essentially identical in the 233-265-residue recombinations of hHO.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of polypeptidic truncation, substrate structure and axial ligand on the active site structure of heme oxygenase.
the molecular structure of the active site of heme oxygenases and its relationship with the molecular structure and electronic properties of the heme substrate.

the influence of polypeptides on the structure of heme, and the influence of heme on the structure of the protein matrix, and the influence on both of environmental conditions, such as pH, temperature and solvent.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the cyanide-inhibibed complex of HO, the substrate PH is tilted towards the protein interior by 1 A, and is oriented such that the vinyls are in a hydrophobic environment.

the molecular structures of the active sites of the recombinant constructs, hHO-233 and hHO-265, with the PH substrate in either the aquo or cyanide-ligated complexes are very similar, but not identical, and that the steric tilt, and therefore the extent of substrate seating, is influenced by the substrate structure, as well as the axial ligand.

the active site molecular structure of the two heme oxygenase constructs, and the PH orientation isomers are essentially identical, but the cyanide-inhibition of the 233-residue heme oxygenase construct results in a significant steric tilt of PH, as determined by NMR.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the absence of axial ligand, the electronic and molecular structure for the active site in the 233- or 265-residue constructs of hHO is essentially identical, but that the cyanide-inhibition of the PH substrate complex is accompanied by a significant change in the PH orientation in the protein, with the major isomer corresponding to the only isomer found in rHO crystals.

the electronic and molecular structures of heme oxygenases, and hence their reactivity and product distributions, are sensitive to the axial ligand, and that the heme substrate is oriented with the vinyls towards the hydrophobic protein interior, and the alpha,gamma axis is tilted towards the protein exterior.

the active site structure of hHO is very robust, with the substrate orientation being the only variable, and that the substrate seating is determined primarily by the steric tilt and orientation of the Fe-CN bond.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the substrate seating of PH in hHO is not significantly altered by the presence of either the N-terminus or C-terminus, by the introduction of axial cyanide or water ligands, or by the replacement of vinyl groups with methyl groups.
the electronic and molecular structure for the PH substrate in the active site of hHO is largely independent of polypeptide chain truncation and substrate modification.

solution NMR is a powerful tool for probing the molecular details of substrate binding and orientation in heme oxygenase, and that the spectral complexity can be managed to yield meaningful information.
